title: Capstone Part 1 - Architecture and Design
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 1 — Architecture and Design ##### The rebuild that a diagram would have prevented A team spent seven weeks building a multi-tenant automation platform. In week eight, during a security review, someone asked how tenant isolation worked. The answer was "every query filters on `tenant_id`." The reviewer asked what happened if a query forgot. Nobody had an answer, because the decision to rely on application-level filtering had never been *made* — it had accumulated. Retrofitting row-level security meant touching every table, every query, and the connection-pooling layer. Three weeks of rework. The cost of that omission was not the RLS implementation, which takes a day. It was that the decision was invisible, undiscussed and unrecorded until it was expensive to change. **Architecture is the set of decisions that are hard to reverse**, and Part 1 exists to make those decisions deliberately, in writing, before code makes them for you. ##### Requirements and success metrics Start with functional scope, then the non-functional requirements that actually constrain the design. Write functional requirements as capabilities with acceptance criteria: ```text FR-1 Ingest webhooks from Shopify, Stripe and a support desk, verified and deduplicated FR-2 Enrich each event against a canonical customer record FR-3 Classify support tickets with AI and route by confidence FR-4 Generate and deliver invoices as PDFs FR-5 Provide per-tenant configuration and isolated credentials FR-6 Expose usage and cost per tenant ``` Then the NFRs, **as numbers**, because these are what eliminate architectures: ```text Volume 3,000 events/day baseline, 15,000 peak (sale days) Latency webhook ack < 200 ms p95; end-to-end < 5 min p95 Availability 99.5% monthly (≈ 3.6 h error budget) Durability zero event loss; every event traceable end to end Tenancy 25 tenants at launch, 200 within 18 months Residency Indian tenants' PII must remain in India Cost < ₹25,000/month at baseline volume Team two engineers, one part-time; must be operable by one on-call ``` That last line is a real constraint and is regularly omitted. An architecture requiring a dedicated platform team is the wrong architecture for two engineers, however elegant. **Success metrics** must be measurable and baselined before you build: | Metric | Baseline | Target | How measured | |---|---|---|---| | Manual processing hours/month | 140 | < 20 | ops time log | | Median first-response time | 6.2 h | < 15 min | ticket timestamps | | Data-entry errors/month | ~12 | 0 | monthly audit | | Cost per 1,000 events | — | < ₹700 | platform usage table | | AI auto-handled share | 0% | > 55% at ≥0.85 confidence | `ai_decisions` | ##### Component-level architecture selection The central design skill is choosing the right tool **per component** rather than adopting one for everything. | Component | Choice | Why | |---|---|---| | Webhook ingestion | FastAPI service | Sub-200 ms ack, HMAC verification, custom dedup | | Event distribution | Redis Streams | Already operating Redis; volume far below Kafka's threshold | | Orchestration | n8n (queue mode, self-hosted) | Connector breadth, per-execution pricing, data residency | | Long-running journeys | Temporal | Multi-day waits with approvals; must survive restarts | | RAG + agent | Python service | Needs tests, evals in CI, cross-encoder reranking | | State + audit | PostgreSQL + pgvector | Transactions, RLS, and vectors in one system | | Scheduled reporting | n8n cron | Simple, visible, low volume | | PDF generation | Python service | Library-dependent, deterministic arithmetic | Two decisions there deserve their reasoning stated. **pgvector rather than a managed vector database**: the corpus is under 200k chunks, and keeping vectors transactionally consistent with relational data in one system removes an entire class of sync problems — worth more than the marginal performance of a dedicated store at this scale. **Redis Streams rather than Kafka**: at 15,000 events on a peak day, Kafka's operational cost buys nothing the team can use. Record what you **rejected** and why. "We chose n8n" is a statement; "we chose n8n over Zapier because 9 steps × 15,000 peak events would cost ₹50,000/month on per-task pricing, and over Make because Indian data residency requires self-hosting" is a decision. ##### C4 diagrams The C4 model gives you four zoom levels; two or three are usually enough. **Level 1 — System context.** Who uses it and what it talks to. ```mermaid flowchart TD U[Ops team] --> P[Automation Platform] C[Tenant admins] --> P P --> S[(Shopify)] P --> ST[(Stripe)] P --> ZD[(Support desk)] P --> CRM[(HubSpot)] P --> LLM[(LLM provider)] P --> SL[(Slack)] ``` **Level 2 — Containers.** The deployable units and how they communicate. This is the most valuable diagram and the one to spend time on. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph EDGE["Edge"] GW[Caddy / API gateway
TLS · rate limit · correlation ID] end subgraph APP["Application"] ING[Ingestion service
FastAPI · HMAC · dedup · 202] N8N[n8n queue mode
main + workers + webhook] TMP[Temporal
long-running journeys] AI[AI service
FastAPI · RAG · agent · evals] PDF[Document service
FastAPI · invoice rendering] end subgraph DATA["Data"] PG[(PostgreSQL 16
+ pgvector · RLS)] RD[(Redis
streams · cache · queue)] VA[(Vault
per-tenant credentials)] end subgraph OBS["Observability"] PR[Prometheus] --- GR[Grafana] LO[Loki] --- GR LF[Langfuse
LLM traces] end GW --> ING & N8N ING -->|persist then publish| PG & RD RD --> N8N N8N --> AI & PDF & TMP AI & PDF & TMP & N8N --> PG AI & PDF & N8N --> VA ING & N8N & AI & PDF --> PR & LO AI --> LF ``` **Level 3 — Component.** Draw this only for the most complex container — usually the AI service. Two supporting artefacts matter as much: a **sequence diagram** for the critical path (webhook → ack → queue → worker → AI → approval → action), and **API contracts** as OpenAPI specs for every internal service, written before implementation so the interfaces are agreed rather than discovered. ##### Data model and canonical schema ```sql -- Tenancy and isolation CREATE TABLE tenants ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, plan TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'standard', region TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'in', -- data residency created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); -- Ingestion: the event ledger and idempotency boundary CREATE TABLE events ( event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, -- provider's ID = dedup key tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id), source TEXT NOT NULL, event_type TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL, received_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending','processing','done','failed','dead')), attempts SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, trace_id TEXT -- correlates across services ); CREATE INDEX idx_events_pending ON events (received_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- Canonical entity: one shape, many sources CREATE TABLE customers ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id), email CITEXT NOT NULL, full_name TEXT, lifecycle_stage TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'lead', source TEXT NOT NULL, source_record_id TEXT NOT NULL, source_updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) ); ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON customers USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant', true)::uuid) WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant', true)::uuid); ``` The design choices worth defending in the document: **the provider's event ID as primary key** (idempotency enforced by the database), **canonical customer with provenance** (avoiding N² mappings), **RLS with `FORCE` and `WITH CHECK`** (the decision the opening story omitted), and **`trace_id` on the event** (end-to-end traceability across five services). ##### Security and multi-tenancy boundaries Document the boundaries explicitly, because they are the decisions most expensive to retrofit: - **Database** — RLS on every tenant-scoped table; application role without `BYPASSRLS`; transaction-scoped `set_config` for pooling safety. - **Credentials** — per-tenant Vault paths with policies; the database stores references only. - **Cache and queue** — tenant ID in every key and message; workers re-validate rather than trust. - **Residency** — Indian tenants pinned to Indian infrastructure; `tenants.region` drives routing. - **AI** — untrusted content (tickets, documents) never reaches a component holding write tools; approval gates enforced in routing code. - **Audit** — append-only log of every consequential action, tenant-tagged. ##### Architecture Decision Records An **ADR** captures one decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences. Three or four for a capstone is right. ```markdown # ADR-002: Enforce tenant isolation with PostgreSQL row-level security **Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-03-14 **Deciders:** platform team ## Context The platform serves 25 tenants at launch, growing to ~200. Tenant data shares tables. A single missing `WHERE tenant_id = ...` in any query — including a join condition — exposes one tenant's data to another. NFR requires provable isolation for a client security review. ## Options considered 1. **Application-level filtering only.** Zero infrastructure change; isolation depends on every query, forever, being correct. One omission is a breach. 2. **Schema-per-tenant.** Strong isolation; migrations run N times; Postgres degrades past a few hundred schemas — conflicts with the 200-tenant target. 3. **Database-per-tenant.** Strongest isolation and enables per-tenant residency; operationally infeasible for two engineers at 200 tenants. 4. **Row-level security (chosen).** Database enforces the predicate on every statement including joins; a forgotten filter returns zero rows, not other tenants' rows. ## Decision Adopt RLS with `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, both `USING` and `WITH CHECK` policies, an application role without `BYPASSRLS`, and transaction-scoped `set_config('app.current_tenant', ..., true)` for connection-pool safety. Reserve option 3 for enterprise tenants with contractual residency requirements. ## Consequences + Isolation is enforced by the database, not by developer discipline. + Satisfies the security review with a demonstrable control. + Automated tests can query without filters and assert zero cross-tenant rows. − Every tenant-scoped table needs a policy; missing one is a silent gap → mitigated by a CI check asserting RLS is enabled on all such tables. − Small per-query planning overhead; measured at <3% on our access patterns. − Debugging in psql requires setting the tenant explicitly (documented in runbook). ``` The value of the format is the **options considered** and **consequences** sections. They record that alternatives were weighed and that costs were accepted knowingly — which is what a reviewer, a successor, or you in nine months actually needs. ##### Risk, cost, and trade-off analysis | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | |---|---|---|---| | LLM provider outage | Medium | High | Gateway with cross-provider fallback + circuit breaker | | Cost overrun from AI | Medium | Medium | Per-tenant budgets, caching, small-model routing, alerts | | Cross-tenant data exposure | Low | Critical | RLS + automated isolation tests in CI | | Peak-day volume 5× baseline | High | Medium | Queue-mode workers autoscaled on queue depth | | Single-engineer bus factor | High | High | ADRs, runbooks, mock handover in Part 4 | | Vendor API breaking change | Medium | Medium | Anti-corruption layer per source + contract tests | ```text COST MODEL (baseline 3,000 events/day ≈ 90,000/month) VPS 4 vCPU/8 GB (n8n + services) ₹ 2,400 Managed Postgres 2 vCPU/4 GB + backups ₹ 3,200 Redis (managed, small) ₹ 900 LLM: 55,000 classifications × ~₹0.12 ₹ 6,600 Object storage + egress ₹ 600 Monitoring (self-hosted Grafana stack) ₹ 800 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Infrastructure subtotal ₹14,500 Engineering ops ~6 h/month ₹ 9,000 TOTAL ₹23,500 (target < ₹25,000 ✓) ``` Include the sensitivity: at 5× volume the LLM line dominates, which is why caching and model routing are in the design rather than deferred. ##### Common pitfalls - **Diagramming the happy path only** — show error paths, queues and approval gates. - **NFRs as adjectives** ("scalable", "secure") rather than numbers. - **One tool for everything** instead of per-component selection. - **No rejected alternatives**, leaving decisions unjustifiable later. - **Data model designed after the workflows**, which is how RLS gets retrofitted. - **Ignoring the team constraint** and designing something two engineers cannot operate. - **No baseline measurement**, making success unprovable. - **Skipping the cost model** until the first invoice. - **ADRs written retroactively** to justify what was already built. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: produce a full **design document** with **C4 diagrams, data model, tool-selection rationale, and cost/risk analysis**, and **defend three decisions as ADRs**. Write the NFRs first and as numbers — they should visibly eliminate options in the sections that follow, which is how you know they are doing work. The mini project is that document, complete and reviewable. Put it in your capstone repository as `docs/01-architecture.md` with the ADRs in `docs/adr/`, so Part 2 onward can reference decisions by number. For the assignment, write **three ADRs** and defend them. Choose decisions that were genuinely contested — tenancy isolation, orchestrator choice, vector store, sync versus async boundaries — not settled ones. Then do the step that makes this exercise real: **have someone challenge them**. An ADR that survives an argument is a decision; one that has never been questioned is a preference with formatting. ##### Key takeaways - Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse; make them explicitly and in writing before code makes them implicitly. - Write non-functional requirements as numbers — volume, latency, availability, residency, cost, and team size — because they are what eliminate candidate designs. - Select tools per component and record what you rejected and why; a decision without alternatives is not a decision. - Design the data model, tenancy boundaries and security controls before workflows, since retrofitting isolation is far costlier than building it in. - Capture contested choices as ADRs with context, options and consequences — including the costs you knowingly accepted and how you will mitigate them.
